questions.q: What is the primary goal of computer forensics?
choices: To identify, preserve, recover, and analyze digital evidence
questions.why: Computer forensics covers the full evidence lifecycle: identifying, preserving, recovering, and analyzing digital evidence in a legally sound way. Data recovery alone is only one piece of that process.

questions.q: Which of the following is a volatile data source?
questions.why: RAM loses its contents the moment power is removed, making it volatile and a priority for live collection. Hard drives, USB drives, and CD-ROMs retain data without power.

questions.q: What is the first step in the forensic investigation process?
questions.why: Investigators must first identify what evidence exists and where it resides before anything can be preserved or analyzed. Preservation and documentation follow once evidence has been identified.

questions.q: Which of the following tools is commonly used for disk imaging in a forensic investigation?
questions.why: EnCase is a commercial forensic suite widely used to create and analyze forensic disk images. Wireshark, Nmap, and Metasploit are network and penetration testing tools, not imaging tools.

questions.q: Which of the following is considered a best practice when handling digital evidence?
choices: Always work on the original evidence
Create a bit-for-bit copy of the original evidence
Use any available tool for analysis
questions.why: Working from a bit-for-bit copy preserves the original evidence in pristine condition and keeps it admissible. Analyzing the original risks altering timestamps and data.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a write blocker in forensic investigations?
choices: To protect the original evidence from modification
To wipe the data on the drive
questions.why: A write blocker allows read-only access to a drive, guaranteeing the acquisition process cannot alter the original evidence. Any write to the source could undermine its integrity in court.

questions.q: Which of the following is a hashing algorithm commonly used in forensic investigations?
questions.why: MD5 has long been used in forensics to fingerprint files and verify that copies match originals. RSA, DES, and AES are encryption algorithms, not hash functions.

questions.q: Which of the following actions should be taken first when seizing a computer at a crime scene?
choices: Document the state of the computer
Access all files on the computer
questions.why: Before touching anything, investigators photograph and document the scene, including what is on screen and how equipment is connected. This preserves context and supports the chain of custody.

questions.q: What type of attack involves an attacker manipulating a file system to gain unauthorized access?
questions.why: Directory traversal manipulates file paths, such as ../ sequences, to escape intended folders and reach restricted files. SQL injection and XSS target databases and browsers, not the file system.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the chain of custody in forensic investigations?
choices: A record of who accessed the evidence and when
A legal agreement between two parties
A physical chain used to secure evidence
questions.why: The chain of custody documents every person who handled the evidence, when, and why, proving it was never tampered with. Without it, evidence can be challenged and excluded in court.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a forensic disk image?
choices: To capture an exact replica of the original media
To remove malware from a system
questions.why: A forensic image is an exact, sector-level replica of the original media, including deleted files and slack space. A normal backup copies only active files and misses that hidden data.

questions.q: Which tool is commonly used for analyzing network traffic in a forensic investigation?
questions.why: Wireshark captures and dissects network packets, making it the standard tool for network traffic analysis. EnCase, FTK, and Autopsy focus on disk and file system forensics.

questions.q: Which file system is commonly used on Windows operating systems?
questions.why: NTFS is the default file system for modern Windows, supporting permissions, journaling, and large volumes. FAT32 is older and limited, while HFS+ and Ext4 belong to macOS and Linux.

questions.q: Which of the following is a primary challenge when collecting evidence from cloud environments?
questions.why: Cloud data may be stored across data centers in multiple countries, raising jurisdiction and legal access problems. Knowing and reaching the data's physical location is the core challenge.

questions.q: What does the ACPO Good Practice Guide primarily provide for digital forensics?
choices: Principles for handling digital evidence so it stays admissible
A standard file format for storing forensic disk images
A certification program for forensic examiners
A software tool for imaging mobile devices
questions.why: The ACPO Good Practice Guide sets out principles, such as not altering data on a seized device, that keep digital evidence admissible in court. Evidence file formats, examiner certifications, and imaging tools are separate things.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a 'dead' forensic acquisition?
choices: Capturing data from a powered-on system
Capturing data from a system that has been powered off
questions.why: A dead acquisition images storage after the system has been powered down, so the data cannot change during capture. Live acquisition, by contrast, collects from a running system.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes steganography?
choices: The practice of hiding data within other files
The encryption of data using a key
The method of securely deleting files
questions.why: Steganography conceals data inside other files, such as images or audio, so observers do not even know a message exists. Encryption scrambles content but does not hide its existence.

questions.q: Which type of forensic analysis is used to recover deleted files?
questions.why: Deleted files often remain on disk until overwritten, and file system analysis examines structures and unallocated space to recover them. Memory and network analysis look at RAM and traffic instead.

questions.q: Which of the following is a tool used for mobile device forensics?
questions.why: Cellebrite specializes in extracting and decoding data from smartphones and other mobile devices. EnCase and FTK are primarily computer forensics suites, and Wireshark analyzes network traffic.

questions.q: Which of the following is a method for securing the chain of custody of digital evidence?
choices: Keeping evidence in a locked, secure location
Sharing evidence with colleagues for analysis
Allowing access to the evidence by anyone
Modifying evidence to fit the investigation
questions.why: Storing evidence in a locked, access-controlled location ensures only authorized, documented handling occurs. Open access or modification would break the chain of custody instantly.

questions.q: Which of the following file types is most likely to contain hidden data?
questions.why: JPEG images are a favorite carrier for steganography because small pixel changes are invisible to the eye. Plain text and HTML files offer far less room to hide data undetected.

questions.q: Which of the following tools is used to analyze the Windows registry?
questions.why: RegShot takes before-and-after snapshots of the Windows registry and compares them to reveal changes. It is purpose-built for registry analysis, while FTK Imager focuses on acquisition.

questions.q: Which file format is commonly used for forensic disk images?
questions.why: E01 is the EnCase evidence file format, which stores a forensic image along with compression, checksums, and case metadata. PDF, JPEG, and DOCX are document and image formats.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a hash value in digital forensics?
choices: A random number assigned to a file
A unique identifier generated by an algorithm for a file
questions.why: A hash is a fixed-length value computed by an algorithm that uniquely represents a file's contents. Any change to the file produces a different hash, which is why it is not random.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a forensic write blocker?
choices: To prevent the system from booting
To prevent changes to the evidence during analysis
To encrypt data on the disk
questions.why: A write blocker's job is to stop any write commands from reaching the evidence drive, so examination cannot change its contents. Cloning and encryption are separate functions.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a logical acquisition?
choices: Capturing an image of the entire hard drive
Capturing only the files and directories visible to the user
questions.why: A logical acquisition copies the files and folders the operating system exposes, not the entire raw disk. It misses deleted files and unallocated space, which require a physical image.

questions.q: Which of the following file systems is most commonly used in Linux?
questions.why: Ext4 is the default file system on most modern Linux distributions. NTFS and FAT32 are Windows formats, and HFS+ is Apple's legacy file system.

questions.q: What must be maintained to ensure digital evidence remains admissible in court?
questions.why: An unbroken chain of custody proves the evidence presented in court is the same evidence collected and was never altered. The other options are networking and storage concepts.

questions.q: Which of the following describes a 'live' forensic acquisition?
choices: Acquiring data from a powered-off system
Acquiring data from a system that is currently running
questions.why: A live acquisition collects data while the system is still running, capturing volatile evidence like RAM, sessions, and running processes. Powering off first would destroy that data.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a forensic investigation?
choices: The process of collecting, preserving, and analyzing digital evidence
The process of performing penetration testing
questions.why: A forensic investigation is the structured process of collecting, preserving, and analyzing digital evidence for legal or internal proceedings. Penetration testing evaluates security, not evidence.

questions.q: Which of the following is used to verify the integrity of a disk image?
questions.why: Hashing the original and the image and comparing the values proves the copy is identical to the source. Matching hashes demonstrate the image was not altered; encryption offers no such proof.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a forensic image?
choices: A compressed copy of the original disk
A bit-for-bit copy of the original disk
An encrypted copy of the original disk
A backup copy of the original disk
questions.why: A forensic image duplicates every bit of the source media, including deleted data and slack space. Compressed or backup copies do not guarantee that complete, exact reproduction.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the concept of steganography?
choices: Hiding data within other files or images
questions.why: Steganography hides information inside innocuous carrier files so its very existence goes unnoticed. Encryption protects content but openly signals that secret data is present.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the role of a forensic examiner?
choices: To collect, analyze, and present digital evidence in legal proceedings
To perform penetration testing on networks
To monitor network traffic for security threats
To design and implement security policies
questions.why: A forensic examiner collects, analyzes, and presents digital evidence, often testifying about findings in legal proceedings. Penetration testing and policy design are security roles, not forensic ones.

questions.q: Which hashing algorithm was historically the most widely used for verifying forensic images?
questions.why: MD5 was the de facto standard for verifying forensic images for many years due to its speed and universal tool support. Collisions have since pushed the field toward SHA-256, but MD5 was the historical workhorse.

questions.q: Which of the following is a potential issue when using cloud services in forensic investigations?
choices: The physical location of the data
questions.why: Data in the cloud can physically reside in foreign jurisdictions, complicating legal authority, subpoenas, and access. This location problem is more fundamental than speed or cost.

questions.q: Which of the following is a tool commonly used for network forensics?
questions.why: Wireshark is the standard tool for capturing and examining network traffic during network forensics. EnCase, FTK, and Autopsy are geared toward disk and file analysis.

questions.q: Which of the following is a key concern when handling digital evidence?
questions.why: Digital evidence is easily altered, so preventing and detecting tampering is the central concern; a single change can render it inadmissible. Cost and size are practical issues, not integrity issues.

questions.q: Which of the following is the purpose of a forensic analysis?
choices: To analyze and interpret digital evidence
To modify data for future use
questions.why: Forensic analysis interprets recovered digital evidence to reconstruct events and support conclusions in an investigation. Recovering data is a step along the way, not the end goal.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common file format used in digital forensics?
questions.why: E01 is the widely used EnCase evidence format for storing forensic images with integrity checks. NTFS, FAT32, and HFS+ are file systems, not evidence file formats.

questions.q: Which of the following is an important consideration when collecting digital evidence?
choices: The speed of the collection process
The preservation of the evidence integrity
The cost of the collection process
questions.why: Evidence integrity must be preserved from the moment of collection, since altered evidence loses its value in court. Speed and cost matter far less than an intact, verifiable copy.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a live forensic analysis?
choices: Analyzing data from a system that is powered off
Analyzing data from a system that is currently running
Analyzing data from a forensic image
questions.why: Live forensic analysis examines a running system to observe volatile data such as memory, processes, and network connections. Analyzing images or powered-off disks is dead analysis.

questions.q: Which of the following is a tool used for memory forensics?
questions.why: Volatility is an open source framework built specifically to analyze RAM dumps, extracting processes, connections, and injected code. EnCase, FTK Imager, and Autopsy center on disk evidence.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the chain of custody?
choices: A record of who accessed the evidence and when
A legal agreement between two parties
A physical chain used to secure evidence
questions.why: Chain of custody is the documented trail showing who possessed the evidence, when, and what they did with it. It is a record, not a physical restraint or an encryption method.

questions.q: Which of the following is a challenge when collecting evidence from cloud environments?
choices: The physical location of the data
questions.why: The physical location of cloud data creates jurisdictional and legal hurdles, since data may sit on servers in multiple countries. Retrieval speed and cost are secondary concerns.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the purpose of a forensic write blocker?
choices: To prevent the system from booting
To prevent changes to the evidence during analysis
To encrypt data on the disk
questions.why: By blocking write commands to the evidence media, a write blocker guarantees examination cannot modify the original. This preserves integrity, which cloning or encryption alone cannot ensure.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common method for securing the chain of custody of digital evidence?
choices: Keeping evidence in a locked, secure location
Sharing evidence with colleagues for analysis
Allowing access to the evidence by anyone
Modifying evidence to fit the investigation
questions.why: Locked, controlled storage with documented access keeps the custody record intact and rules out unauthorized handling. Sharing freely or modifying evidence would destroy its admissibility.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a 'dead' forensic acquisition?
choices: Capturing data from a powered-on system
Capturing data from a system that has been powered off
questions.why: Dead acquisition means imaging media from a system that is powered off, ensuring nothing changes during capture. It sacrifices volatile data like RAM in exchange for a stable source.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a live forensic acquisition?
choices: Acquiring data from a powered-off system
Acquiring data from a system that is currently running
questions.why: Live acquisition captures evidence from a running system, which is the only way to obtain volatile data such as memory contents and active connections before they vanish.
